Theme

Playground equipment, sandbox toys, vehicles and play · Travel & transport

mount verb

a horse

also get on a horse, climb into the saddle, dismount, get off a horse

classical

Cic. Sen. 34: in equum omnīnō nōn ascendere

in equum ascendere

ascendō, ascendere, ascendī, ascēnsum, with in + accusative

mount a horse

Cicero’s phrase; Livy has equum ascendere with the plain accusative (Liv. 23.14, Lewis & Short). To get off is ex equō dēscendere (Cicero, below).

Other words

  • equum cōnscendere — mount a horse

    cōnscendō, cōnscendere, cōnscendī, cōnscēnsum, with accusative · also used · classical · Liv. 29.2.16; Ov. M. 14.820: equōs (Lewis & Short)

    Livy and the poets; cōnscendere is chiefly to go on board a ship (see get on, of a bicycle).

  • in equum īnsilīre — jump onto a horse

    īnsiliō, īnsilīre, īnsiluī, with in + accusative · also used · classical

    Comenius’s rider (below) jumps on.

  • ex equō dēsilīre — dismount, jump down from a horse

    dēsiliō, dēsilīre, dēsiluī, dēsultum · also used · classical · Caes. BG 4.2.3: ex equīs (Lewis & Short)

    Caesar’s Germans leap down to fight on foot.

Examples

  • cum ingressus iter pedibus sit, in equum omnīnō nōn ascendere; cum autem equō, ex equō nōn dēscendere

    once he has set out on foot, he never gets on a horse at all; once on horseback, he never gets offCic. Sen. 34

  • Deinde īnsilit in equum, indit pedēs stapedibus, sinistrā capessit lōrum (habēnam) frēnī

    Then he jumps onto the horse, puts his feet in the stirrups and takes the rein of the bridle in his left handComen. OP 83

See also horse riding, ride, get on, climb up.

SourcesLewis & Short: ascendo · Lewis & Short: conscendo · Lewis & Short: insilio · Lewis & Short: desilio · Lewis & Short: descendo

Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica, loci-comenius), checked against the editions named there.

Livy, Ovid and Caesar as Lewis & Short quotes them. Comenius is post-classical (stapēs, stirrup, is a modern word).
